title: Building Efficient Universal Classifiers with Natural Language Inference
authors: Moritz Laurer, Wouter van Atteveldt, Andreu Casas, Kasper Welbers
text:
Over the past year, generative models have taken both academia and public attention by storm. The main appeal of text generation is that it is so universal, that almost any other text-related task can be reformulated as a text generation task [1,2]. Especially when text generators are massively scaled up and tuned on human instructions, they acquire impressive capabilities to generalise to new tasks without requiring task-specific fine-tuning [3,4,5,6,7]. Since the utility of these generative Large Language Models (LLMs) has become evident, large amounts of intellectual, financial and energy resources are being invested in improving and scaling generative LLMs.

Given that the resource requirements for training and deploying generative LLMs are prohibitive for many researchers and practitioners, this paper investigates other types of universal models, that make a different trade-off between resource requirements and universality. The literature has developed several other universal tasks that cannot solve generative tasks (summarization, translation etc.), but can solve any classification task with smaller size and performance competitive with generative LLMs [8,9].

The principle of universal classifiers is similar to generative models: A model is trained on a universal task, and a form of instruction or prompt enable it to generalize to unseen classification tasks. While several efficient approaches to universal classification exist [10,11,12,8,13,14,15], this paper focuses on guidance for one approach: Natural Language Inference. Several papers have used the universal NLI task for zero- and fewshot classification, but stopped short of mixing NLI data with multiple other non-NLI datasets to build more universal classifiers [16,17,18,19].

The main contribution of this paper are: (1) easy-to-use universal classifiers trained on 5 NLI datasets and 28 non-NLI datasets with 389 diverse classes, improving zeroshot performance by 9.4% compared to NLI-only models; (2) a step-by-step guide with Juypter notebooks enabling users to train and adapt their own universal classifiers.
